questions.scenario: GET /api/v1/accounts/{number} is protected with hasRole('CUSTOMER'). A tester logs in as customer A and requests customer B's account number. B's balance is returned.
questions.question: What vulnerability is this, and how should it be fixed?
options: Broken object-level authorisation: check that the account belongs to the caller (ideally by querying with the customer ID) and return 404 otherwise
Broken authentication: require a stronger password
SQL injection: use prepared statements
CSRF: enable CSRF tokens
questions.explanation: The role check is correct but says nothing about which account. Every access to an owned object must verify ownership; querying by number and customer ID makes other customers' data unreachable.

questions.scenario: A service class has a public method transferAll() that loops and calls this.transfer(...), where transfer is annotated with @PreAuthorize.
questions.question: Is the @PreAuthorize check applied to these inner calls?
options: Only when running tests
Only if transfer is private
Yes: annotations always apply
No: method security works through a proxy, and calls on this inside the same class bypass it
questions.explanation: Spring's proxy intercepts calls coming from outside the bean. Self-invocation goes straight to the method, so the check must be on the entry point or in another bean.

questions.scenario: The update-profile endpoint binds the request body directly onto the Customer JPA entity. A customer sends {"email": "new@example.com", "kycTier": 3}.
questions.question: What is the risk?
options: Mass assignment: the customer raises their own KYC tier; use a DTO containing only the fields customers may change
The request will always fail with 400
None: JPA validates every field
Denial of service
questions.explanation: Binding to entities exposes every property, including ones only staff should set. Role-specific request DTOs prevent it.

questions.scenario: A teller initiates a ₦20,000,000 transfer. Policy says transfers above ₦5,000,000 need approval by a different supervisor.
questions.question: Where must the 'maker cannot be the checker' rule be enforced?
options: In the database backup process
In the server-side approve operation, comparing the approver with the maker, and recording both in the audit trail
Only in the web UI by hiding the Approve button for the maker
In the mobile app
questions.explanation: Controls enforced only in a UI can be bypassed by calling the API directly. Segregation of duties must be checked where the action is executed, and audited.

questions.scenario: A multi-tenant banking-as-a-service platform reads the tenant from an X-Tenant-ID header sent by the client.
questions.question: What is the safer design?
options: Encrypt the header
Derive the tenant from the authenticated token's claims and filter every query by it (with row-level security as a second defence)
Let each tenant choose a hard-to-guess tenant ID
Keep the header but document it clearly
questions.explanation: A client-controlled header can simply be changed. The tenant must come from verified identity, and database-level policies add defence in depth.

questions.scenario: You are designing authorisation for a support agent role.
questions.question: Which practices follow least privilege? (Choose two.)
options: Support agents get the ADMIN role so they are never blocked
Support agents can read customer profiles with sensitive fields masked, but cannot move money
Privileged actions such as unfreezing an account require a reason and are audited with the agent's own user ID
Support agents share one 'support' login to save licences
questions.explanation: Least privilege gives only the access a job needs and keeps actions attributable. Shared logins destroy accountability, and blanket admin rights defeat the model.

questions.scenario: A team keeps adding @PreAuthorize expressions such as "hasRole('SUPPORT') or (hasRole('CUSTOMER') and @repo.findById(#id).get().owner == authentication.name)" across many services.
questions.question: What improvement makes this safer and easier to maintain?
options: Remove method security and rely on URL rules
Disable the checks in production for performance
Move the logic into a dedicated authorisation bean (or custom annotation) with its own unit tests, and reference it from the expressions
Copy the expression into every method for consistency
questions.explanation: Complex SpEL strings are hard to read and impossible to unit test. A bean centralises the rule, can be tested directly, and is reused through simple expressions or a meta-annotation.
